title: COGTINUUM: 2500 KM Through the Desert on All Gravel Fixed Gears – Donnet Dumas & Stan Engelbrecht
content:
Stan Engelbrecht and three friends are about to take four custom-built steel fixed-gear bicycles along an all-gravel backroads route from the center of Namibia to Cape Town. They’re calling the adventure COGTINUUM. Read on for Stan’s description of the project below accompanied by beautiful 35 mm film photos from Stan Engelbrecht and Donnet Dumas. Hop on, it’s gonna be a wild ride…

It started with a dream in July 2024. An actual dream, dreamt while sleeping in a tent, under a huge tree whose branches dripped with scorpions, in a dried-up riverbed in Namibia.

A few days later, as we drove over the crest of the Fish River Canyon and dipped onto the flat, moonscape heading back home, I finally spoke the dream aloud …

Eventually, that weird dream, with me stuck in a support car feverishly trying to get out to join my friend Nkosi as he flew through the desert, mashed together with a few other ideas that had been grinding around in my head for a while. And on 8 October 2024, a late-night text to my friend and fellow fixed gear rider Nick McIntyre laid out the bare bones:

Four riders.

Fixed gears.

Steel frames.

No brakes.

Iron ore train.

Namibia to Cape Town.

Who could pass on that? Now we just needed some more riders. And the bikes. And some money. (And a whole lot of other shit, it would turn out).

For over a year I emailed out the proposal document to many, many, many companies, collaborators, photographers, filmmakers… pretty much anyone, to see if someone would get on board with us:

“I’m writing to you about a bit of a crazy project … myself and a handful of experienced and dedicated fixed gear riders are undertaking a month-long 2500km ride from the little town of Omaruru in the centre of Namibia all the way to Cape Town, South Africa. We’ll be crossing the red dunes of Sossusvlei, past the Fish River Canyon, Aussenkehr, the Orange River, the Richtersveld mountains, and the desolate South African West Coast on custom-built fixed gear gravel bicycles. It will be an awesome adventure”

Sossusvlei Dunes

It took many conversations to help explain the ‘why’ behind this. Because ‘I had a dream’ doesn’t really cut it in the real world. And eventually I was able to put it into words:

“I’m a long-time steel frame and fixed gear rider, and on a recent touring trip along the remote South African West Coast I encountered the legendary 4-kilometer-long Sishen-Saldanha cargo train that takes iron ore from the interior to the coast for export. This surreal sight led me to make a conceptual link between the physical iron ore and the steel bicycle I was riding, and  the fascinating process that connects these two states of steel …”

 Fish River Canyon

“The overarching theme of the project is the recyclable resource that is steel, and particularly bicycle frame builders that use steel. We will be telling the story of the iron ore that is extracted from the African landscape we’ll traverse, its journey to foundries around the world where it becomes bicycle frame tubing, and how that tubing, in this case, is returned to become bicycle frames, built specifically by Southern African frame builders. These steel frames will become the bicycles we ride from Omaruru to Cape Town. In part, the project aims to highlight the benefits of choosing a steel frame over a carbon frame, while at the same time highlighting the skills of some Southern-African frame builders.”

And the builders are who this is really all about. Ex-Saffron builder Matthew Sowter, a South African based in London, was the first to get on board. He and I worked together on the first frame, getting all the quirky measurements and clearances out of the way for the rest.

David Mercer of Mercer in Cape Town, South Africa, was an obvious choice; I own two of his bikes already. And David always knows I am up to something.

David and Kai

With a bit more digging, I was able to find Zimbabwean Carlos Santa Clara of Santa Clara Bikes (recent recipient of the SRAM Bespoked Inclusivity Sponsorship), based in Lisbon, Portugal. He was in.

And finally, a late entry of new builder Kai Pringle of The Bellum Project, also based in Cape Town, rounded up the builders group nicely. Kai is also going to ride his frame on the trip.

Each of these builders committed to building a steel gravel fixed gear frame with a steel fork.

Which is where Reynolds came in. They generously sponsored the tubing and paved the way to get the project up and running. From the beginning, I had a clear idea of what these bikes should look like.

Sowter details

Conceptually, I foresaw the bikes paying somewhat of a homage to the early track bikes that made it out of the velodromes and onto the city streets around the world in the 1980’s. Paired with components with a classic nod, it would complement the project perfectly. I was seeing these parts with a polished finish, reflecting the arid desert and blue skies of the Namib spectacularly. As for the paintwork, we settled on the idea of leaving them completely unpainted, raw. Letting them rust and patina all the way down to Cape Town. A way to track the passage of time on the raw material. Steel being the star of the show, after all.

Richterveldt Road

Now the hunt was on to spec the frames with nowadays really rare matching all-silver components. Rim manufacturer Astral was the first to see the potential of how beautiful a fully polished rim could look out in the desert. Loren from Astral really got it, and through a massive effort was able to get the rim sets hand-polished for all our bikes. To assist with our tyre clearance issues was Paul Components and their super niche, super beautiful, super polished wider spaced fixed gear hub sets. Ritchey, Alter, Miche, and White Industries were the next obvious choices as manufacturers that still offered anything other than all-black.

Ultradynamico, Fizik, Tailfin and Izumi took our desert rig builds to the next level.

Map Planning

We spent months waiting for all the frames to be completed. And weeks were spent agonizing over the route, planning the most spectacular way down with deconstructed atlases stuck up on a wall. We got together to build wheels, fit tyres, and try out components.

David brazing and wheel building

An all-gravel fixed gear is totally new territory. And we had no idea how these frames would ride. For all we knew, they could be complete dogs. But we had flights and accommodation booked. So… Ha ha! Thank fuck they ride like absolute WHIPS!

Small human in landscape

The project is called COGTINUUM. We’ll be crossing the desert along an all-gravel 2,500 km route on these things. We start on 1 October 2026. This is just the beginning. Follow the adventure over on Instagram.
